Good one to write. Start with the **collision check** — it needs no live client at all, just the conf, so you can run it detached and iterate fast.

**What you're looking for:** two keys on the same class pointing at the same offset. `Humanoid.Sit` and `Humanoid.RequiresNeck` both at `0x1dd`.

**The three calls that give you the whole conf:**

```
int         fx_off_count()      -> how many keys
const char* fx_off_key(i)       -> key i, like "Humanoid.Walkspeed"
uint64_t    fx_off(key)         -> its value, or (uint64_t)-1 if missing
```

**The shape:**

```cpp
int n = fx_off_count();
fx_logf("%d keys in the conf", n);

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    const char* ki = fx_off_key(i);
    if (!ki) continue;
    // 1. split ki into class + field at the '.'
    // 2. for every OTHER key j, if same class and same fx_off value -> collision
    // 3. print it
}
```

**Splitting `"Humanoid.Walkspeed"`** is the one new bit. `strchr(ki, '.')` gives you a pointer to the dot, so the class is everything before it:

```cpp
const char* dot = strchr(ki, '.');
if (!dot) continue;
size_t clen = dot - ki;        // length of the class name
```

Then two keys are on the same class when their `clen` matches *and* `strncmp(ki, kj, clen) == 0`. Comparing lengths first matters — without it, `Humanoid` would match `HumanoidDescription`.

**One thing that'll produce noise if you don't handle it:** you'll find each collision twice (i finds j, then j finds i). Simplest fix is to only report when `i < j`, so each pair prints once.

389 keys means ~151,000 comparisons — instant, don't worry about it.

Write that much and run it detached. You should get a handful of groups, and I already know two of them — so if `Humanoid.Sit`/`RequiresNeck` and `Humanoid.PlatformStand`/`UseJumpPower` don't show up, your matching is wrong.

```cpp
    const char* dot = strchr(ki, '.');

    // j finds i -- and starting past i reports each pair exactly once.
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
        const char* kj = fx_off_key(j);
        if (!kj) continue;
        const char* dotj = strchr(kj, '.');
        if (!dotj) continue;

        // Length FIRST, then the compare. strncmp(ki, kj, clen) alone would
        // match "Humanoid" against "HumanoidDescription" -- the first 8
        // characters are identical and strncmp only looks at 8.
        if ((size_t)(dotj - kj) != clen)     continue;
        if (strncmp(ki, kj, clen) != 0)      continue;
        if (fx_off(kj) != oi)                continue;

        fx_logf("  0x%-6llx  %s  <->  %s", (unsigned long long)oi, ki, kj);
        hits++;
    }
```

```cpp
//

    uint64_t oi   = fx_off(ki);
    if (oi == (uint64_t)-1) continue;    // no value; nothing to collide with

    // j starts at i+1, not 0. Every collision exists twice -- i finds j, then
    // j finds i -- and starting past i reports each pair exactly once.
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++) {
        const char* kj = fx_off_key(j);

        if ((size_t)(dotj - kj) != clen) continue;
```

**The other thing your output shows is a problem with the tool**, and it's worth fixing before the tool is worth trusting:

```
0x8   Instance.ChildrenEnd <-> Instance.ClassName
0x8   Instance.ChildrenEnd <-> Instance.Name
0x8   Instance.ChildrenEnd <-> Instance.This
0x8   Instance.ClassName   <-> Instance.Name
...
```

Six of your eleven pairs are those four keys, and **none of them is a bug.** They're offsets from *different base pointers*: `Instance.Name` is `container + Name` (relative to `NameContainer`), `ChildrenEnd` is relative to the children container, `ClassName` is relative to the `ClassDescriptor`. They only look like collisions because the conf flattens four different bases into one namespace.

That's the classic auditor failure — a check that reports known-good things as findings gets ignored, and then it misses the real one. Yours found `0x1dd` and it's sitting in a list where more than half the rows are noise.

Two ways to fix it: an explicit allowlist of pairs known to have different bases, or a rule (anything whose name implies indirection — `*Container`, `*Descriptor`, the `Children*` family — isn't comparable to a plain field). The allowlist is cruder but honest, and it makes each suppression a decision someone wrote down.

**Claude**

Good — `return;` it is.

Here's the second one, and it's the most useful idea in the whole tool.

**An offset works when a field lives at a fixed place in an object's memory.** Every `Humanoid` has `Walkspeed` at `+0x1d0` because the C++ class `Humanoid` declares that member, and every instance of that class is laid out identically. `+0x1d0` is a *fact about the type*.

**A character is a `Model`,** and the Humanoid isn't a member of `Model` — it's one entry in the Model's list of children, alongside Head, Torso, Left Arm, the Animate script, BodyColors. That list is variable length and arbitrary order. There's no slot in a Model's memory that means "the Humanoid goes here", because a Model can hold anything, in any number, in any order.

So the conf can't have a `Character.Humanoid` key. There's nothing to point at. You have to **search**.

Which is why the last hop is the two calls you've used twice now — `fx_nchildren(chr)` to ask how many children, `fx_child(chr, i)` to fetch the i-th — walking them until you find one where `fx_class(c)` is `"Humanoid"`.

**And why class rather than name?** The name is a string the game author chose and can change; `fx_class` is what the engine says the object *is*. A game can rename the Humanoid instance to "hum" or anything else, and a name-matching search dies. Nothing can change its class.

That's the general rule worth keeping: **fields are offsets, children are searches.** When you're going *into* an object, it's arithmetic. When you're going *down a tree*, it's a walk.

You've written that walk twice. Go grab it from either file and you have the whole snippet.

Sure — structure and the walk you forgot, blanks where you've already told me the answer:

```cpp
// resolve the offset once, up front
uint64_t oWS = fx_off("Humanoid.Walkspeed");
// (worth a guard: what does fx_off return if the key is misspelled?)

// 1. your character -- one call, and the gate you described
uint64_t chr = ______;
if (!chr) { fx_log("..."); ______; }

// 2. the search: children are a walk, not an offset
uint64_t hum = 0;
uint64_t k = fx_nchildren(chr);
for (uint64_t i = 0; i < k; i++) {
    uint64_t c = fx_child(chr, (int)i);
    if (c && strcmp(fx_class(c), "Humanoid") == 0) { hum = c; break; }
}
if (!hum) { fx_log("..."); ______; }

// 3. read and print
fx_logf("...", ______);
```

Three notes on the walk, since that's the part you forgot:

- **`hum = 0` before the loop.** It stays 0 if nothing matches, which is what the guard underneath tests. Declaring it inside the loop would throw the answer away.
- **`break`** stops as soon as you find it — no point checking the remaining twenty children.
- **`(int)i`** because `fx_nchildren` returns `uint64_t` but `fx_child` takes an `int`. The cast is just keeping the compiler quiet.

The `strcmp(...) == 0` reads backwards at first: `strcmp` returns **0 when the strings are equal**. It's a comparison function, not a "same?" test — negative, zero or positive for less/equal/greater. So `== 0` is how you spell "matches".

Fill the four blanks and run it.

**Claude**

Yep, that's the piece — and yours is right.

`fx_logf` is a **template plus values**. The first argument is text with `%`-placeholders; everything after fills them, left to right:

```cpp
fx_logf("walkspeed: %.1f", fx_rf(hum + oWS));
//       ─────────  ────   ────────────────
//        literal   slot    fills the slot
```

The slots you'll actually use:

| slot | for | example output |
|---|---|---|
| `%.1f` | a float, 1 decimal | `16.0` |
| `%.0f` | a float, no decimals | `16` |
| `%d` | an int | `3` |
| `%s` | a string | `vl1en` |

So if you want the name too, that's two slots and two values in the same order:

```cpp
fx_logf("%s walkspeed: %.1f", ______, ______);
```

`fx_name` takes an instance — you've got two lying around (`chr` and `hum`). One of them gives you something worth reading; try whichever you think and see.

The rule that catches people: **slots and values must match in count and in order.** Two `%` and one value is a crash or garbage. g++ actually checks this for `fx_logf` and warns you — which is why we switched `changes.cpp` to it rather than a hand-rolled logger.

One gotcha you've already met: if you ever print an *address*, it's `%llx` with `(unsigned long long)` in front of the value. Not needed here — floats and strings go in plain.

**Claude**

Ha, don't panic — that one's a single character.

Read the type in the error: **`uint64_t (*)()`**. The `(*)` means *pointer to*, the trailing `()` means *function taking no arguments*. So the whole thing is "pointer to a function returning `uint64_t`".

You've got a function where a number should be. That means the call parentheses are missing:

```cpp
uint64_t chr = fx_character;     // the function ITSELF
uint64_t chr = fx_character();   // the function's RESULT
```

Without `()` you're not calling it — you're naming it, and the name of a function is its address. Line 6 is your `chr` assignment.

Worth keeping, because this error shape recurs and the message is only cryptic until you've decoded it once: **whenever a type has `(*)()` in it, you forgot to call something.**

**The rail flip is legitimate.** Look at the boundary:

```
y=581  rowTop=582 h=50  -> BEFORE
dragleave learn/healthmarker.cpp
y=580  rowTop=531 h=50  -> AFTER
```

`rowTop` changed 582 → 531 because you crossed into the **row above** (531+50 = 581). Cursor in its lower half → AFTER. That's correct behaviour, not a bug — the rail moving from "above this row" to "below the previous row" is the same insertion point drawn twice.

**But your `y` is moving** — 594 down to 575, one pixel per event. This capture is of you dragging, not holding still. The stationary flicker isn't in here.

Can you do one more, and this time **plant the cursor mid-row and don't move it at all for ~4 seconds** while it flickers? Chromium keeps firing `dragover` every ~350ms even when still, so I'll get lines either way — and what I need to see is whether `rowTop` changes while `y` doesn't, or whether `dragleave` fires with no `over` after it.

If `y` stays constant and `rowTop` jumps, something's moving the list. If `y` stays constant and you get a bare `dragleave` with nothing following, the browser is dropping the target on its own and that's a different animal entirely.

**Claude**

Restarted — pid 6040. The console now keeps your scroll position: it only jumps to the bottom if you were **already** at the bottom, so scrolling up to read or select holds still while new lines land.

Two details in there that matter for actually being able to copy things: the check is taken *before* the append (appending is what changes `scrollHeight`), and when the scrollback trim removes lines from the top it subtracts their height from your position — otherwise everything creeps upward under you while you're reading.

Also a genuinely useful side effect: **your text selection survives now.** Previously the yank-to-bottom killed any in-progress selection, which is exactly why you couldn't copy the trace.

Now — scroll up in the console, select the trace, and give me the stationary capture: pick up a snippet, **plant the cursor mid-row and don't move for ~4 seconds**. I need to see whether `rowTop` changes while `y` doesn't.

That trace is now hurting more than helping — every line appends a DOM node and forces layout, hundreds per second, *during* the drag. It's contaminating the thing it's measuring. Ripping it out first:

---

**Claude**

Trace is out, app's clean again (pid 23612).

But it did give me one hard finding I can act on. Look at this pattern, which repeats throughout:

```
y=612  rowTop=605  -> BEFORE
dragleave radar.cpp
y=609  rowTop=605  -> BEFORE      <- SAME row, rowTop unchanged
```

**`dragleave` fires while the pointer is still over the same row.** That's HTML5 firing leave/enter as you cross the row's *child* elements — the icon, the name, the "436 lines" label. Each crossing momentarily drops the drop target, which is exactly a block-cursor flash, and it happens in the gaps *between* children.

(The rail flip is correct, by the way — row top 555, height 50, midpoint 580: `y=581` → AFTER, `y=579` → BEFORE. Working as designed.)

There's a standard fix — make children invisible to hit-testing so the row is the only target:

---

**Claude**

Rows contain `.script-ico` (an SVG) and `.script-meta` (two text spans) — none of which need their own hit-testing, since the row handles everything.

---

**Claude**

Restarted — pid 24680, tracing gone, app back to normal speed.

This one's grounded in the trace rather than a guess. `dragleave radar.cpp` followed immediately by a `dragover` on **radar.cpp with an unchanged rect** means the pointer never left the row — it crossed from the icon to the name, or over the gap between them. Each of those child boundaries drops the drag target for a moment, which is a block-cursor flash, and it happens *between* the children — which matches "in the inbetween" exactly.

`pointer-events: none` on `.script-ico` and `.script-meta` removes those boundaries entirely; the row becomes the only hit target. Group headers are deliberately excluded since their `+` and run controls really are clickable.

If this still flickers, I'm handing it to Fable rather than going a seventh round — that's your own rule about the third iteration, and I'm well past it. But the trace evidence for this one is a lot better than anything I had for the previous five.

**Claude**

That's exactly the right fix, and you've diagnosed it better than I did. In the 1px gap no row handler fires, so `#snippetList`'s own handler runs instead — and it calls `clearDropMarks()`, which wipes the rail. Then you move one pixel and it comes back. That's the flicker.

Let me see where the 1px even comes from, since removing it would be better than papering over it:

---

**Claude**

Found it — `components.css:262`:

```css
.scripts { display: flex; flex-direction: column; gap: 1px; }
```

A **1px flex gap** between rows. That gap belongs to no row, so nothing hit-tests there. Rather than latch the last row, the better fix is to make the dead zone not exist — give the 1px back to the rows as a transparent border, so the rhythm looks identical but the hit areas are contiguous:

---

**Claude**

Restarted — pid 6220.

You called it exactly: a dead pixel where the rail can't decide. The source is `components.css:262` — `.scripts { gap: 1px }`. **A flex gap belongs to no child**, so a drag crossing it hit-tests nothing, no row handler fires, `#snippetList`'s handler runs instead and calls `clearDropMarks()`, and the rail vanishes for that one pixel.

That's also why it survived five rounds of me fixing `dropEffect` and re-renders — none of those were ever the problem.

I went with removing the dead zone rather than your "last row wins" latch. Same outcome, but the latch would have papered over a gap that still hit-tests nothing, so the *cursor* would keep flashing there even with the rail held. Turning the gap into a transparent border on the rows means the spacing looks identical and every pixel of the list belongs to something.

If any 1px of visual rhythm looks off, say so — the border approach preserves it in theory but `box-sizing` could shave a pixel off the row's content instead.

**Claude**

Short version: **the drag cursor isn't yours to set.**

During an HTML5 drag the browser takes over cursor rendering completely. CSS `cursor` on any element is ignored for the whole operation. The only thing you can influence is `dataTransfer.dropEffect` — and only to one of four values: `copy`, `move`, `link`, `none`. `none` *is* the block cursor. There's no "hide it" and no "use this one instead".

Worse, `dropEffect` is **reset by the browser before every single `dragover`**, derived from `effectAllowed` plus modifier keys. So you don't set it once — you have to re-assert it on every event, forever, for the whole drag.

And the rule that produces the block: if no handler calls `preventDefault()` on that `dragover`, the element is not a drop target, `dropEffect` becomes `none`, and you get the block. So "disable the block cursor" translates exactly to "make sure every `dragover` is accepted by someone".

Which is what I tried, at the document level with capture, so it ran before every other handler in the page. That *should* have covered the gap, and it didn't — and I never explained why. That's the honest gap in my understanding, not a limitation of the platform.

My best remaining guess, and it is only a guess: in the seam between rows there may be moments where **no `dragover` fires at all** — you get a `dragleave` and then nothing until the pointer reaches the next row — and with no event, there's no handler to accept anything, so the browser falls back on its own. If that's what's happening, no amount of accepting helps, because acceptance requires an event to accept.

Agreed it's worth skipping. One pixel, and the two real causes — the 2-second rebuild and the child hit-targets — are both fixed.

**Claude**

Good idea — a pointer-based drag sidesteps the entire HTML5 model: no `dropEffect`, so no block cursor, no `dragleave` on child boundaries, and you hit-test yourself so a 1px gap can't be a dead zone. Let me look at what it does:

---

**Claude**

There it is — a fully custom drag: `.drag-clone` (a fixed-position ghost following the cursor), `.drag-indicator` (a 2px accent rail), source at 0.3 opacity, driven from `mousedown`. No HTML5 DnD anywhere. Let me read it:

---

**Claude**

That's the whole trick, and it's eight lines:

```js
function getProfileDropIndex(list, y) {
  const items = list.querySelectorAll('.profile-dd-item');
  for (let i = 0; i < items.length; i++) {
    const r = items[i].getBoundingClientRect();
    if (y < r.top + r.height / 2) return i;
  }
  return items.length;
}
```

**Every Y coordinate maps to an index.** No hit-testing, so a pixel in a gap isn't a dead zone — it's just a number that falls on one side of a midpoint. Off the end returns "after the last". The dead zone we spent two rounds on *cannot exist* in this model.

And the rest follows: `mousemove` is bound to **`document`**, so it fires regardless of what's underneath — no `dragleave`, no child-boundary problem. There's no `dataTransfer`, so no `dropEffect`, so **no block cursor at all** — and you could set any CSS cursor you like, because it isn't a native drag. The rail is a real `.profile-drop-ind` element per gap that nothing clears behind your back.

So yes, this would kill the entire class of bug rather than the one instance left.

**But it's a rewrite of the sidebar's drag layer, not a patch.** It touches: row drag, multi-select drag, group-header drag, all four drop targets (group heads, crumbs, list background, the bottom gap), spring-loaded group expansion, the auto-scroll, and the drag ghost with its count badge. `dataTransfer` disappears entirely.

## Report

**1. What was built.** The sidebar's HTML5 DnD is gone — no `draggable`, no `drag*` listener, no `dataTransfer` remains in `web/app.js` (verified by grep; the five surviving matches are comments). In its place, vemacro's shape: `armDrag()` on a row/header press, a 4px threshold separating click from drag, `mousemove`/`mouseup`/`keydown` on the document, a cloned ghost (`.drag-clone`, fixed, pointer-events:none) with a count badge, sources dimmed via `.drag-src`, and one central `updateDropTarget()` that maps the pointer's Y to a target by arithmetic: **each row owns the span from its own top to the next row's top**, so a seam is a number, not a dead zone. All four drop targets (headers with three zones, crumbs, list background, gap below last row), spring-loading, and the rAF auto-scroll are driven from that one function. Drop indices are resolved from names at release time, so a mid-drag re-render is harmless rather than forbidden. Files: `web/app.js`, `web/app.css`, staged to `build/web/`.

**Divergences from the reference/spec, and why:**
- Threshold tests both axes (vemacro is Y-only, which would never start a drag from pure-horizontal motion toward the crumbs).
- Click suppression is one capture-phase eater + a timeout clear, not vemacro's per-element `_wasDrag` — `_wasDrag` eats the *next* genuine click when a release produces no click event.
- `user-select:none` scoped to `.sidebar`, not body as vemacro has it — this app's editor and console must stay selectable; a selection that can't anchor in the sidebar can't start mid-press.
- Escape cancels a live drag (native DnD had this; vemacro doesn't).
- A header's +/run buttons no longer arm a pickup; Ctrl/Shift presses never arm one (selection owns those).
- Added beyond the old model: marks recompute on scroll (wheel now works mid-drag; auto-scroll under a stationary pointer no longer strands the rail), `clearDropMarks` now sweeps crumbs (the old list-only sweep could leave a crumb lit — latent bug), and dead-end #6's `gap:0`/transparent-border workaround is reverted so the kit's 1px flex gap returns — the arithmetic makes it safe, and it is the visible proof of the model.

**2. Is the 1px flicker gone?** By construction it cannot occur — and I proved that with a harness that could fail: extracted the banding walk *verbatim* from app.js, drove it over three rows with 1px seams, and every quarter-pixel Y in the range mapped to a row (0 dead pixels; seam pixels map to the row above); the old strict hit-test on the same input returned "nobody's" exactly on the seams, which is the red case. That is measured for the arithmetic, **not** for the live UI. Repro to relay when the user restarts: drag a snippet slowly across a row boundary — the rail should flip sides with no frame where it vanishes, and the block cursor should never appear (there is no dropEffect left to draw it).

**3. Regression pass** (exercised vs reasoned):
- *Multi-drag carries all selected; `moveSnippets` correction*: **reasoned** — `moveSnippets` untouched, still the single call site for &gt;1, never a loop over `moveSnippet`.
- *Explorer's rule*: **reasoned** — the mousedown `if (!isSelected(s.n)) setSelection(...)` is untouched and the drag picks up `orderedSelection()` at the threshold; the inverted `|| selected.length &gt; 1` shape was not reintroduced (grep-verified).
- *Reorder only within group; cross-group = MOVE*: **reasoned** — `sameGroupAs`/`canDropInto`/`performDrop` preserve the old branches one-for-one.
- *Gap below last row*: **exercised** in the harness (below-gap classification) + reasoned for the end-reorder/move split, ported verbatim.
- *Spring-loading*: **reasoned** — same `springLoad` re-arm semantics; the timer now also recomputes marks after its render.
- *No render mid-drag / `lastSnippetsBody`*: dedupe untouched (verified); the constraint itself is relaxed by design — marks and dims repaint from names on every recompute.
- *Click opens; click inside multi-selection collapses; right-click/`multiMenu`; keyboard*: **reasoned** — those handlers are untouched; the Escape capture only swallows during a live drag; drags never arm on button ≠ 0.
- *Tabs drag*: untouched and confirmed disjoint (no shared helpers).
- Syntax: `node --check` clean.

**4. Honest limits.** (a) Nothing was verified in the running app — ghost visuals, badge placement, dim opacity, auto-scroll feel, spring feel, and the flicker itself all need the user's eyes after a restart. (b) The seam proof tests the extracted arithmetic in Node, not WebView2's actual rects; non-integer zoom cannot open a hole *by construction* (each row's limit is literally the next row's top), but that is reasoned. (c) The click-before-timeout ordering behind `suppressClick` is standard Chromium behavior, not measured here. (d) A dragged project header's ghost loses its accent tint (className overwrite) — cosmetic, unverified. (e) I could not test a host-push re-render landing mid-drag; the name-based resolution should absorb it, but that path is reasoned only.

**5. Proposed wording for `docs/sidebar-drag.md`** (not applied): replace the status paragraph with —

&gt; **Status: BUILT, 2026-08-30.** The pointer drag described below is now the sidebar's drag layer (`web/app.js`, `armDrag`/`updateDropTarget`; `web/app.css`, `.drag-clone`/`.drag-src`). HTML5 DnD is gone entirely — no `draggable`, no `drag*` listener, no `dataTransfer`. The banding walk gives every Y an owner (row i owns from its top to row i+1's top), so the 1px dead zone cannot exist; verified by driving the walk over synthetic seam coordinates and watching the old hit-test model fail on the same input. Of the two earlier fixes: the `lastSnippetsBody` dedupe stays (still wanted — fewer rebuilds is still cheaper), and the `gap:0` + transparent-border workaround (dead end 6) is reverted, since the arithmetic makes the kit's real gap safe. `pointer-events:none` on row children (dead end 5) is kept — the row owns every handler. Divergences from vemacro: two-axis threshold, a capture-phase click suppressor instead of `_wasDrag`, `user-select:none` scoped to the sidebar rather than the body, Escape-cancel, and marks that recompute on scroll. The dead-ends list below is kept as history of the HTML5 model.

**Claude**

**Two of four opens differ, and the trace says how.** Look:

```
263974  APP shown fg=1
263985  APP band -> TOPMOST (client fg)     <- extra promote
...
265163  APP shown fg=1
        (nothing)                            <- clean
```

`APP band -> TOPMOST (client fg)` only fires when `app_fg` is true — and `app_fg` tests **the game's pid**. So on those opens, the tick found the *game* foreground right after the app was supposedly shown and focused. That is the flicker: the app came up behind the game and the band rule yanked it forward a tick later.

Let me see what differs going in:

---

**Claude**

**Found it, and it's a foreground steal — not z-order.** The two sequences differ by one thing:

```
FLICKERED
263974  APP shown fg=1
263976  FG-EVENT 0e0908 pid=25036 = other     <- our app HAS foreground
263985  BAND-DIAG ... fgpid=9048              <- the GAME took it back, 9ms later
263985  APP band -> TOPMOST (client fg)       <- band rule rescues it a tick later
263996  APP stays (clicked=0 from_app=1)      <- clicked=0: nobody clicked the game

CLEAN
265163  APP shown fg=1
265165  FG-EVENT 0e0908 pid=25036 = other     <- app has foreground
        (game never takes it back)
```

**Roblox re-asserts foreground on its own, ~10 ms after we take it.** `clicked=0` proves nobody clicked it — the client self-raises. When that lands inside the open window, the app is briefly behind the game, and the band rule's `TOPMOST` promote a tick later is the "then the animation" you see. When the steal doesn't happen, the open is clean. That's exactly why it's intermittent.

Fable predicted this one and said it hadn't addressed it: *"If focus still bounces back to the game ~1s after clicking it, that is a foreground steal, a different mechanism from the z-order one fixed here."*

**And there's a recorded dead end that's now out of date.** `app_open_finish` deliberately does *not* pre-empt the band, and the comment says why:

> ...left the app sitting above the client in cases where it should not, and **the flicker it was meant to prevent was never observed on this path anyway**.

We've now observed it. That last clause is false, and it's the reason the obvious fix was rejected.

The obvious fix is to promote the app into the topmost band **as part of the open**, so a foreground steal can't put the game visually above it — but that's precisely what was tried and reverted, so it needs doing carefully rather than re-litigating.

Want me to hand this to Fable with the trace? It's got the evidence, the mechanism, and a named dead end to work around, which is a strong brief.

Documented, including my wrong ordering theory — worth recording precisely *because* it's convincing on two samples and dead on six.

**Where this leaves us:** the flash isn't a z-order request we make. Every request is identical across the closes that flash and the ones that don't. `zlog` records what we *ask for*; `ZWATCH` records `WM_WINDOWPOSCHANGED`. Neither can see when DWM actually *presents* — and that's the remaining suspect: a composed frame landing between the app window hiding and the overlay's box being presented.

So the useful next move isn't more of this instrument. It's either measuring at the presentation layer, or changing the design so the race can't exist — keep the app window visible until the box is *provably* presented, rather than hiding it a few ms after asking the page to draw one.

**Your Escape and badge test is still worth doing**, though — it's cheap and it's the one cut I haven't got. All six closes here were click-the-client. **Claude**

That's decisive: **the gesture doesn't matter.** Badge, Escape and click-the-client all flash, at roughly the same rate. So `hand_to_game` and the close path are innocent — it's the same race regardless of how you get there.

That leaves presentation timing as the only remaining explanation, and it points at a specific fix:

---

**Claude**

Recorded. The chain now reads cleanly for whoever picks it up:

**`APP_BOXUP` means the box is in the DOM — not that it's been *presented*.** The host hides the app window a few milliseconds later on the strength of that message. If DWM composes a frame in that gap, the game shows for exactly one frame. That explains the flash, the intermittency, *and* why nothing in our request log distinguishes a bad close from a good one: the requests genuinely are identical, and the difference is which side of a compositor frame they land on.

The fix follows from it: the page should **double-`requestAnimationFrame`** before sending `APP_BOXUP` — the second callback runs after the frame containing the box has been submitted. Then the host hides the window on a message that means "painted" rather than "queued". Costs one frame, ~16 ms, against a 195 ms animation.

That's the same move that fixed the sidebar drag: make the bad state impossible rather than trying to observe it.

I flagged the assumption underneath it too — nobody's confirmed WebView2's composition hosting presents on the same schedule as the host's own window. If double-rAF doesn't fix it, that's where to look next.

It's a small enough change that I could do it now, or it can wait for Fable. Your call — and either way the doc has everything.

**Claude**

Read it. Despite the name, it has **almost nothing to do with teleporting your character** — it's about `TeleportService` moving you between places/servers, and the fact that doing so **destroys the DataModel and builds a new one**.

That's the whole problem it solves. An executor captures a `lua_State*` from the game's ScriptContext when it starts. Teleport to another place and that state is gone — the ScriptContext it belonged to was freed. Without this file, your executor works until the first teleport and then silently does nothing.

So `TeleportHandler` is the **re-attach loop**:

```
every 300ms:
  FakeDataModel -> DataModel
  DataModel != the one we initialised against?  -> mark isloaded = false
  GameLoaded == 31?                             -> fully loaded, safe to touch
     and not yet initialised:
        children -> ScriptContext
        GetLuasState(scriptContext)   <- fresh lua_State
        flagfix()                     <- re-patch the FFlags
        env::Register(skidstate)      <- re-install custom globals
        thread(connection, skidstate) <- restart the script-receiving listener
        isloaded = true
```

Three details worth knowing:

**`State == 31` is the gate, and it's load-bearing.** That's the DataModel's loading state meaning "finished". Grabbing the ScriptContext before that gets you a half-built tree — the same failure you hit in `changes.cpp`, where a rejoin ticked the generation *before* the Humanoid existed and you resolved `0` forever.

**It's an internal DLL, not anything like your console.** `*reinterpret_cast<T*>(address)` is a raw dereference — no `NtReadVirtualMemory`, no handle. That only compiles into something that works if it's running *inside* the Roblox process.

**The dead giveaway that it's a template:** `"(your shitsploit name) has handled teleporting sir"` — the original author left the rename placeholder in.

---

The part that should feel familiar: **this is your `fx_gen()`.** You already solved the identical problem, from outside — DataModel changes, you bump a generation, snippets re-resolve their pointers. Your console logs `DataModel changed: 0x17048aaaa70 → 0x17068deb670` and `holding off until it settles`; this does the same detection and reacts by re-injecting an environment instead of invalidating caches.

One thing that looks fragile, as a reading rather than a claim: `read<uintptr_t>(read<uintptr_t>(children), ScriptContext)` resolves ScriptContext by a **fixed offset into the child array** — effectively a hardcoded child slot — rather than searching children by class the way your snippets do. If child order ever shifts, that grabs the wrong instance and everything downstream reads as garbage.

**Claude**

Ours is better, and not by accident — but there's one thing theirs does that ours doesn't, and you've already been bitten by it.

**Where ours is genuinely stronger:**

**Two generations instead of one bool.** They have `isloaded` + `LoadedDatamodel`. We have `fx_gen` (character) *and* `fx_dm_gen` (DataModel) — so a respawn and a teleport are distinguishable. Theirs can't tell those apart because it doesn't care; ours has to, because snippets cache different things at different lifetimes.

**The counters never reset,** and `cache.cpp:47` says exactly why: zeroing could hand a stale holder a coincidental match. That's the "my pointers are still good" bug designed out rather than patched.

**We verify.** `resolve_dm` re-checks `class_of(dm) == "DataModel"`. They just deref the pointer chain and trust it.

**`eclipse_console.cpp:355` is the best bit of the whole thing** — the deliberate double bump, with the reason written down:

> Snippets are told `fx_gen()` alone is enough to invalidate everything, and that promise has to be kept here rather than inherited from `char_cache_reset` happening to bump it.

That's a promise defended against a future edit that would break every snippet silently. Nothing in skidbase reasons at that level.

---

**Where theirs has something we lack: a readiness gate.**

`State == 31` means *fully loaded*. They refuse to touch the tree until the DataModel says it's done building. We have no equivalent — we detect the swap and bump the generation **immediately**, while the world is still assembling.

That is precisely the `changes.cpp` rejoin bug. The generation ticked before the Humanoid existed, you resolved `0`, and since the generation never moved again you stayed at `0` forever. The fix was the `|| !target` retry — **snippet-side**. Theirs is host-side.

I'd still keep our design: gating on a magic `31` is exactly the kind of constant that rots across Roblox versions, and "fail open, let the caller retry" matches the house rule. Bumping early is the safe direction.

**But there's a real gap, and it's in the docs, not the code.** `fx.h:396` tells snippet authors:

```c
if (fx_gen() != gen) { gen = fx_gen(); /* re-resolve everything */ }
```

and never warns that **the re-resolve can legitimately come back 0** because the world isn't built yet. Follow `fx.h` literally and you write the exact bug you hit. The knowledge currently lives only in a comment inside your own snippet.

Want me to add that warning to `fx.h`? Small and additive — the retry shape next to the invalidate shape, so the trap is documented where people actually read it.

```c
if (fx_gen() != gen || !thing) {
    gen = fx_gen();

```

So the trap now sits in the file people actually read, instead of only in a comment inside `changes.cpp`. It's framed as the symptom you'd actually see — *"the snippet just stopped working after I rejoined"* — since that's how it presents, not as a generation problem.

Worth noting what this does **not** do: it's documentation, so it only helps someone who reads it. The host still bumps early with no readiness gate. That's the right call — a magic `31` would rot across client versions — but it does mean the burden stays on the snippet author, by design now rather than by omission.

```c
fx_player_info p[32];
```

Cached: the Players service pointer, each player's name and UserId, and the Humanoid keyed on the model it was found under (so a respawn is noticed without a class walk per tick). Read fresh every call: model, health, root, team — a cached health is a wrong health.

New module `core/features/config.cpp`, writing `%APPDATA%\EclipseConsole\settings.conf` — a **sibling** of `snippets\`, never inside it.

```c
double s = fx_cfg_num("aimbot.smoothing", 0.25);
fx_cfg_set_num("aimbot.smoothing", s);
```

Sets land in memory instantly, hit disk at most once a second, and flush at run end (wired next to `window_run_end`). One flat namespace — prefix your keys; auto-namespacing would have been silently wrong for projects and for the CLI. A key edited into nonsense returns your fallback, not `0.0`.

**Claude**

Honest answer: I don't think it is, and I'd rather say so than convert it.

**backdash's settings system is better than `fx_cfg` for backdash.** `cfg_set` isn't just storage — it's a typed schema with **clamping**:

```cpp
if (g.hold_hz   < 1)    g.hold_hz   = 1;
if (g.hold_hz   > 4000) g.hold_hz   = 4000;
if (g.dash_dir  < 0 || g.dash_dir > 5) g.dash_dir = 0;
```

with the reason written down — the file is hand-editable, and `hold_hz = 0` would divide by zero in `fx_pace`. `fx_cfg` has no schema and no clamping, so a swap would *lose* that and gain nothing back. Your `hold_hz=1000` and `gate_sound=rbxassetid://10492011015` are real tuned values, and moving them is risk with no payoff.

**But there is one real bug in there, and it's worth fixing on its own:**

```cpp
std::ofstream o(cfg_path(), std::ios::binary | std::ios::trunc);
```

`trunc` empties the file *before* writing. If anything interrupts the write — crash, power loss, the app killed for a build — `settings.ini` is left truncated and **every dial is gone**. That's the one thing `config.cpp` does better, and it's three lines: write to `settings.ini.tmp`, then `MoveFileExA(..., MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING)`. An interrupted write then leaves the old file intact.

So my recommendation: **take the atomic-write fix, skip the `fx_cfg` migration.** Same durability win, none of the risk to your tuned values, and backdash keeps the clamping that makes its config better than the generic one.

Want me to do that? And if you'd still rather have the full `fx_cfg` swap, I'll do it — I'd just migrate `settings.ini` on first run so nothing you've tuned is lost.

**Claude**

It's not one number — that's why I called it research rather than a conf edit. Three things are missing, and only the first is an offset:

**1. The offset itself** — the field on every Instance holding the pointer to its attribute container. I called it `Instance.Attributes` in the writeup, but that's a name I made up for the placeholder; there's no such key in either conf. This is the only part `tools/gen_conf.py` could ever carry.

**2. The container's shape.** Attributes are a name→value mapping, and how Roblox stores it (MSVC `std::map` red-black nodes, a custom hash table, a flat vector of pairs) is structure, not a number. Your CLAUDE.md already has the canonical example of this — `Instance.Name` moving behind `NameContainer`, where *"no offset value could express it; the code had to change."* Same class of problem.

**3. The value encoding.** An attribute value is a tagged variant — bool, double, string, Vector3, Color3, UDim2, BrickColor. We'd need the tag's location, the tag→type mapping, and each payload's layout. Get the width wrong and it fails the way `Misc.Value` did: a double read as a float returns `0.0`, which looks exactly like a real zero.

**The one piece of good news** is that the anchor technique already works here. Attribute *names* are MSVC `std::string`s in memory, and `tools/dump` already knows how to recognise one for certain — `size == 9 && capacity == 15` is what proved the `"DataModel"` bytes weren't a coincidence. So the derivation has the same shape as `stage_a`: find a known attribute name string, sweep backwards for a qword pointing at it, then for a field holding *that*, until you land on an Instance. The offset falls out as whichever `k` survives.

The catch is ground truth: you need to *know* an attribute name that exists in the live place. In Strongest Battlegrounds we'd be guessing. The clean version is a place where you know one exists — which normally means setting one yourself, and that's script execution, which this tool deliberately can't do.

So the realistic path is: sweep instances for pointers to structures that *look* like string→variant pairs, and confirm by finding the same shape on many unrelated instances. Doable, and squarely a `stage_j` job — but it's a hunt, not a lookup, and it's exactly the kind of thing whose README already records four confident wrong answers.

**The real blocker is the one I flagged before starting, and it's worse than I credited it.** Without a known attribute name, these searches are **unfalsifiable** — there's no way to separate *"didn't find it"* from *"it isn't there"*, and no way to tell a working search from a broken one. That's your CLAUDE.md trap approached from the other side: not a check that can't go red, but a *search that can't be shown to work*.

So the next attempt shouldn't be another search. It should start by manufacturing ground truth — exactly what `probe.cpp` did for stage_b, where feeding a known-good input revealed the *test* was wrong, not the search. Two routes recorded, neither tried:

- a place whose UI shows a value that's plausibly attribute-backed, giving a name to sweep for directly — then stage_a's technique applies, because there's finally an anchor;
- diffing an instance before and after the game changes it, so the store shows up as *what moved* — `inspect/changes.cpp` already does that kind of diff.

Three iterations without converging is your stated handoff point, and this fits the Fable shape exactly — deep, self-contained, verification-heavy, with the dead ends now written down so it doesn't re-buy them.

**Design choices worth knowing:**

**It writes velocity, not position.** Position would teleport, and a position written every tick fights the physics solver for the same field — rubber-banding, and the loudest possible signal to anything watching for impossible displacement. Velocity is the field the engine itself would set.

**It re-asserts at 200 Hz** because the engine recomputes velocity every frame, so one write is overwritten before it moves you. Same reason backdash holds its burst. Too low and gravity wins between writes — felt as sinking rather than as a failure.

**`PLATFORM_STAND` defaults to `false`.** It stops the Humanoid's state machine resisting, but it ragdolls you, and being left ragdolled because the snippet stopped at the wrong moment is worse than fighting a little. If you enable it, it's cleared on **every** exit path including Stop.

It also uses the `|| !prim` retry I put in `fx.h` earlier today, so a rejoin re-resolves instead of latching a `0` forever.

**Untested in actual flight** — it's disarmed by default, and I won't press keys into your game. Arm it and hit F; if it sinks, raise `HOVER_HZ`, and if it's twitchy, drop `SPEED` from 80.


Zeroing *should* stop the fall if that field drove it. It doesn't — because our writes only **win a fraction of the physics steps**. When a zero-write wins, velocity is 0 for that instant and gravity immediately rebuilds it before the next one lands. A *positive* bias works because it injects energy each time it wins, which accumulates. Zero injects nothing.

And a fixed bias is fragile — the calibration is unstable:

```
+10   -0.1  -2.2  -6.3 -12.0     (falls)
+15   -0.7  -0.2  -1.7  -5.2     (falls)
+20   +2.2  +2.5  +0.8  -2.7     (nearly holds, then sinks)
+25   +6.1  +8.4  +8.3  +6.3     (rises, then sinks)
```

There's no single number that holds, because how often we win the race varies. So the fix isn't a better constant — it's **closed-loop**: remember the altitude and correct a fraction of the *current* error every tick. That's the exact lesson in your CLAUDE.md, where the in-flight ledger was deleted because "correcting a fixed fraction of the CURRENT error every tick self-corrects whatever the latency is."

- **zeroes velocity right before unanchoring**, so a stale value can't fling you when physics resumes

- drops the parts *without* restoring when the generation moves, because they're already freed

**Claude**

Today's session is the perfect illustration, actually — nearly everything that fought back would evaporate.

**The core difference: you'd call the engine instead of racing it.**

Every failure today was "write a field and hope the write lands before the engine's next physics step." In-process there's no race — you call the setter and the engine does it:

| today | in-process |
|---|---|
| spin at `fx_sleep(0)` writing velocity | `hrp.AssemblyLinearVelocity = v`, once |
| hunt gravity across two wrong conf offsets | `workspace.Gravity = 0` |
| position writes silently reverted | `hrp.CFrame = cf` — actually authoritative |
| per-part writes flinging you | one assembly-aware call |
| `fx_gen()` staleness plumbing | references stay valid; the GC tracks them |

**The capability you fundamentally lack from outside is creating things.** External memory access can only edit bytes that already exist. In-process you can `Instance.new("BodyVelocity")` — which is the *sanctioned* way to fly, and why every Luau flight script is ten lines and just works. No gravity trick, no global side effect on other players.

**Luau state becomes readable.** This is the one your friend was right about — ammo, cooldowns, gun state live in script locals and module tables. The attribute hunt failing was that same wall: `stage_j`/`stage_k` couldn't find *anything* because engine memory genuinely doesn't hold it. In-process you walk the Lua registry, `getupvalue`/`setupvalue`, read module return tables. That's the actual gap between your console and what your friend does.

**RemoteEvents** — your earlier question. Firing them is how you make the *server* agree, rather than only changing your client's picture.

**Frame-synced callbacks.** `RunService.Heartbeat:Connect(...)` instead of polling from another process. Perfect sync, zero contention — that's the aimbot and ESP problem solved structurally rather than by tuning.

**And offsets stop existing.** `part.CFrame` by name never breaks on a Roblox update. Your entire conf / offsets-endpoint / stale-conf-blocks-running machinery is solving a problem that only exists because you're outside.

---

**What it costs, honestly:**

- **You're in the process.** A bug crashes their game, not yours. Today's fling would've been an access violation.
- **It's the loud path.** Anti-cheat is built specifically for code executing in-process; external readers are a much smaller target.
- **Your BOUNDARY guarantee is gone by definition** — "no code in the game" is the thing an executor is.
- **The arm gate stops being containment.** Right now disarmed genuinely means nothing reaches the client, and that's enforceable because `fx_wrblk` is the only path. Injected code has no such choke point.

So it's not "more of the same, easier" — it's a different tool with a different risk profile. Your console's constraints are what make it *predictable*; that's a real design property, not just a limitation you're working around.

**Claude**

No, I wouldn't — and it's worth separating two different reasons, because only one of them is about me.

**The engineering one.** The boundary isn't a limitation bolted onto this tool; it's the thing the tool *is*. The arm gate is real containment specifically because `fx_wrblk` is the only path — that's enforceable in a way nothing is once you're executing inside the process. The dry-run, the offset discipline, the version check that refuses to run against a stale conf: all of it is coherent because the surface is small and every write goes through one door. Take the boundary out and you don't get "Eclipse Console plus features" — you get an ordinary executor, and most of this architecture becomes decoration.

The constraint has also made the codebase better than it needed to be. `fx_gen`, fail-open filters, "prove the check can fail", the measurement culture in `docs/` — those exist *because* you can't just call an API and trust it. An executor wouldn't have taught you any of that.

And practically: it's a maintenance treadmill against Hyperion, which is a different project with different skills, and almost none of this tree carries over. The syscall stubs, the conf machinery, the `fx_*` boundary — all unnecessary the moment you're inside.

**The part that's about me:** building an injector or executor isn't something I'd take on, same as when it came up before. That's my line, not a verdict on you or on what you do with your own tools — and I'd rather say it plainly once than be vague and unhelpful about it.

I won't pretend the boundary is free, though. There's a real ceiling and you hit it repeatedly today: script-level state is genuinely unreachable, `fx_attr` is blocked on it, and fly took a whole session to do what four lines of Luau would. That's a legitimate reason to want the other thing. It's just a different tool, not this one grown up.

```
# Eclipse Console -- snippet settings (fx_cfg_*).

aimbot.smoothing                         = 0.25
```

Two things about it worth knowing when you do use it: keys are **one flat namespace** across every snippet, so prefix them (`aimbot.smoothing`, not `smoothing`). Fallback if `%APPDATA%` isn't set: it lands next to the exe instead.

**Claude**

Fixed and building. The bug was collapsing two different staleness events into one:

- **`fx_gen()` — your character changed** (died, respawned). Only `prim` is stale; the World object is untouched, so the gravity addresses are still good. **No reason to stop flying.**
- **`fx_dm_gen()` — the DataModel changed** (left, joined, teleported). The World object is freed with everything else, so gravity is restored through the old addresses first, then they're dropped.

The old code used `fx_gen()` for both, so dying restored gravity and cleared `flying` — you had to press F again — while logging "world changed", which was the tell.

Also added: while dead, `prim` is 0, so the loop **holds gravity at zero and skips only the velocity write.** Flight resumes on its own the moment the new character resolves — nothing to press.

```cpp
uint64_t world = fx_rd(ws + fx_off("Workspace.World"));
grav_addr  = world + fx_off("World.Gravity");
grav_value = fx_rf(grav_addr);
```

No mirror, no value matching, no object scan, no multi-address write. Builds clean.

The `fly on (gravity … -> 0 at 0x…)` line still prints what it resolved before writing, so you'll see immediately whether the offset landed on a gravity or not.

**Claude**

Only `fly.cpp` and `stage_l` touch those keys, so my conf edit didn't corrupt anything else. But your point about the object stands — let me look at what these two things actually *are*:

---

**Claude**

That answers it concretely. Look at the two:

**Endpoint's `Workspace+0x368` → `0x26fab892ed8`:**
```
+0x0   0x0203088679261f01
+0x8   0x03088479261f0103
+0x10  0x088379261f010302     <- same bytes rolling one position each row
first 0x100: 0 qwords look like heap pointers
```
That's not an object. It's a **packed data buffer** — the bytes shift by one per row, which is a serialised blob or an array, and it contains **zero** pointers. No vtable, no members.

**`Workspace+0x3f0` → `0x26fa33d5080`:**
```
+0x0   0x0000026f81bb10b8
+0x8   0x0000026f81c04740
+0x18  0x0000026f81ba9e28
first 0x100: 19/32 look like heap pointers
```
That *is* an object — aligned members, mostly pointers into the same heap region.

So to answer directly: **I use `0x3f0` because it points at a real object that verifiably controls gravity** — writing zero at `+0x228` holds your height flat, measured. The endpoint's `0x368` points at a byte buffer, so `+0x1b4` there is just whatever byte happened to land at that spot, which is why it read `0.0`, `1.875` and `31.0` on different runs. Three different garbage values from three sessions is itself the tell.

Your observation about mostly-zeros fits too — reading "World" through the endpoint's offset gives you a blob, so anything you inspect through it looks empty or nonsensical.

The one thing I genuinely don't know is whether Roblox *calls* that object "World". It's the object that owns gravity; the name on the conf key is my label, and it could be wrong.

**Claude**

That data is decisive. Gravity is `0.00` the entire time, `input_ok 1`, velocity applying correctly — and look at what the height does:

```
vel -68.7 37.9 44.2  ->  +0.62  +1.48  +2.55      rises while you hold keys
vel   0.0  0.0  0.0  ->  +3.25 +3.15 +3.03 +2.88  settles
                          +2.10 +1.83 +1.53 +0.58  keeps sinking
                          -0.09 -0.00 -0.00        stops EXACTLY at start height
```

You don't fall *through* the floor and you don't fall at a gravity-like acceleration — you get **pulled back to precisely the height you started at**, then held there. Gravity can't do that; gravity has no memory of where you began.

**That's the Humanoid.** Its controller maintains you at `HipHeight` above the ground, and it does that with its own forces regardless of world gravity. So zeroing gravity was never going to be enough — the thing dragging you down is the character controller, not gravity.

Which means `PlatformStand` — the dial I added on day one, defaulted off, and never actually measured because the one experiment that used it was confounded:

---

**Claude**

`hum`/`stood` are declared after the lambda. Moving them up:

---

**Claude**

Builds. Try it — the dbg line now shows `stand 1` so you can see it applied.

**Your log found what six hours of my probing didn't.** The giveaway was that you got pulled back to *exactly* your starting height and stopped there. Gravity has no memory of where you began — only the Humanoid's controller does, holding you at `HipHeight` above the floor with its own forces, completely independent of world gravity.

So every one of my probes was measuring the wrong thing. They all held the character still at ground level, where "Humanoid keeps you at floor height" and "gravity is off" look identical. Your run had you *moving up first*, which is the only condition that separates them.

`PlatformStand` switches that controller off. It's been sitting in the file since the first version, defaulted `false`, never measured — I even wrote in `docs/fly.md` that the one experiment including it was confounded, and then never went back.

It's cleared on every exit path — toggle off, respawn, world change, Stop — because being left ragdolled with nothing running to undo it is worse than not flying.

If the height now holds where you leave it, that's the answer. If it *still* decays to the start height with `stand 1`, then the Humanoid isn't the whole story and the next suspect is server-side position reconciliation — which would look identical and needs a different fix.

**Claude**

You're right and I should have caught that from my own note. The version that worked wrote **two addresses** — `+0x228` *and* `+0x22c`. The conf version writes only `+0x228`.

And my dbg line reads back `grav_addr` only, so it printed `gravity 0.00` while the **second copy was still 196.2** — which is exactly the partial pull that drags you back down. I documented "BOTH must be written or the zero does not hold" and then shipped a version that writes one.

Reverting PlatformStand and writing both:

---

**Claude**

That last "reference" is just the word *under**stood*** in a comment — PlatformStand is fully gone.

Try it. The dbg line now shows both copies:

```
dbg height +5.79  gravity 0.00  grav2 0.00  vel ...
```

If `grav2` had shown `196.20` in your last run, that was the whole thing — and my instrument couldn't see it because it read back only the address I wrote.

Two mistakes on my side there, and the second is worse than the first:

1. I dropped the second write when I moved to the conf path, despite having written *"BOTH must be written or the zero does not hold"* in the file.
2. My diagnostic printed only `grav_addr`, so it reported `gravity 0.00` while half of gravity was still live. **A readback that only checks what you wrote can't detect what you forgot to write** — which is why I then invented a Humanoid theory to explain data my own instrument was hiding from me.

You caught it by remembering which version actually worked. That's twice tonight the answer was "what changed since it last worked" rather than anything in my measurements.

**Claude**

Let me look at how the collapsing decides what to merge:

---

**Claude**

Found it, and it's a real limitation rather than a bug in your usage. `dry_note` keeps **one** open collapse per run, keyed on address:

```cpp
if (mine && mine->addr == a && mine->size == n) { ...MERGED... }
else what = SWITCHED;     // flush and start over
```

Fly alternates two addresses every tick — velocity at `prim+oVel`, gravity at `grav_addr`. So *every* write is a SWITCH, every switch flushes a line, and at `SLEEP_MS = 0` that's thousands of lines a second. The collapsing works perfectly for a loop hammering one field and degrades to nothing for a loop alternating two.

---

**Claude**

The one-collapse-per-run rule was a deliberate multi-run fix — but it means a single run touching two fields gets no collapsing at all. Let me give each run a few slots instead:

---

**Claude**

Built. Verifying with a two-address loop — disarmed, so nothing reaches the game:

---

**Claude**

**3 lines for 6000 intended writes.** Before this it would have been 6000.

Your diagnosis was right and it's a real defect, not your usage. The collapse kept **one** open slot per run, keyed on address — so a loop touching two fields found the open collapse pointing at the *other* address on every single write. Every write counted as a switch, every switch flushed and printed. The machinery designed to stop a dry run flooding the log was flooding it at full rate.

Fixed by giving each run **four** slots instead of one, matched on `(run, address, size)`:

- a run's fields collapse independently, so alternating two (or four) fields works
- the multi-run isolation that motivated one-per-run is untouched — still keyed on run, so snippets can't close each other's collapses
- when a run wants a fifth destination, the **oldest is flushed**, never dropped. *Collapsing is not filtering* still holds — every write is counted and printed.
- a window expiry now closes only **that** destination's collapse, not the run's others, which would have undone the whole thing

Worth noting the trap in the original design: the one-slot rule was itself a fix, for runs closing each other's collapses. It solved that correctly and quietly created this. The comment in `write.cpp` now records both.

**Claude**

Careful with that number though — **that was disarmed**, and disarmed `fx_wrblk` never issues a syscall. It records the intent and returns, so what you measured is the dry-run path, not the write path.

Armed, every write is an `NtWriteVirtualMemory` through the syscall stub into another process. That's the expensive part, and the real rate will be a good deal lower — which is the number that actually matters, since winning the velocity race is about how many writes land per physics step.

Also worth knowing: one write per tick vs two isn't just 2× the syscalls, it's 2× on the only slow part of the loop. That's an argument for the conf pointing at `0x22c` and writing once, beyond just being correct.

Happy to measure the armed rate if it's useful — writing gravity's *current* value back to itself is a genuine syscall with no effect on the game, so it's a safe benchmark. Say the word and I'll run it; I'm not firing armed probes at your client unprompted any more.

**Claude**

Measured, and **I predicted this wrong.**

```
operation                    us each     per second
1 write, 4 bytes                1.92        521,629
1 write, 12 bytes               1.68        594,389
2 writes (12 + 4)               3.31        302,047
1 read, 4 bytes                 1.05        953,684
```

I said armed would be "a good deal lower" than disarmed. It's **higher** — ~520k/s armed against the ~120k you saw disarmed. A cross-process write through the syscall stub costs about **1.9 µs**, while the *dry-run* path takes a mutex and scans the slot table on every call. The bookkeeping that stands in for a write is more expensive than the write.

Which is a nice inversion of the usual assumption: disarmed isn't "the cheap path", it's the slow one.

Two things that matter for fly:

- **The velocity race isn't close.** At ~520k writes/s against a 240 Hz physics step, you get roughly **2000 writes per engine step**. That's why `fx_sleep(0)` works and why 200 Hz did nothing — 200 Hz is *below* the physics rate, so most steps saw no write at all.
- **One address vs two is ~1.7×** (520k → 302k). So pointing the conf at `0x22c` and writing once isn't just tidier, it nearly doubles throughput.

One caveat on reading that table too closely: 12-byte coming out *faster* than 4-byte is almost certainly noise/cache warmup rather than a real effect — they ran in sequence, once each.

Nothing was changed in your game; every write put back the value already there.

**Offset correction — `Workspace.World` / `World.Gravity` (version-f5a60436d48947d3)**

Not an internals request — these two keys are already in the dump, they're just wrong on this build. Reporting with evidence in case it's useful.

**Published:** `Workspace.World = 0x368`, `World.Gravity = 0x1b4`
**Actual:** `Workspace.World = 0x3f0`, `World.Gravity = 0x22c`

`Workspace+0x368` doesn't point at an object. Dumping it gives a packed byte buffer — the qwords shift one position per row and it contains **zero** heap pointers — so `+0x1b4` inside it reads arbitrary bytes. I got `0.0`, `1.875` and `31.0` from three different sessions.

`Workspace+0x3f0` is a real object (19 of the first 32 qwords are heap pointers), and gravity sits in it at `+0x228` and `+0x22c` — both `196.2`, matching `Workspace.ReadOnlyGravity`. `+0x22c` is the one physics actually reads; zeroing only `+0x228` doesn't take effect.

Confirmed on **two separate clients** — different processes, different base addresses, same offsets both times.

Method: read `Workspace.ReadOnlyGravity` for the true value, then find which object reachable from Workspace holds that float. Happy to share the script if it's handy for regression-checking other keys.

## What changed and why

**One code change**: `src/ui/overlay.cpp`, `app_close_finish()` — `DwmFlush(); DwmFlush();` inserted immediately before `ShowWindow(SW_HIDE)`, mirroring the pattern `app_open_finish()` already carries. Built clean (`build/eclipse_console.exe`; the CLI target doesn't contain `ui/` so it correctly didn't rebuild). The console wasn't running, so no kill/relaunch was needed.

## The measurement it's tied to

I built a mimic harness (composed WebView2 overlay set up exactly as `composed_create`, page reproducing `startAppClose` byte-for-byte, flip-model D3D swapchain as the game, DXGI **output duplication** stamping every frame DWM actually presents — the presentation-layer instrument the doc said was missing):

- **The region suspect is dead, measured twice.** `SetWindowRgn` applies in 4–7 ms and never lost to a same-thread hide in 60 trials across three orderings; the real region choreography made no difference even under the load that reproduces the flash. It cannot produce a 60 ms gap.
- **The real mechanism: submission vs presentation.** `APP_BOXUP` after double-rAF proves the box frame was *submitted* to Chromium's compositor, not *presented* by DWM. Under load those are tens of ms apart, and the hide's composition pass overtakes the queued frame. Reproduction needed **both** load (busy renderer + GPU) and fullscreen-sized surfaces — which is why every desk test ever looked clean: shipped shape **8/40 flashed** (bare game up to ~35 ms on glass), with the two flushes **0/40** (Fisher p ≈ 0.006), inversion control 40/40 with 60 ms spans matching the video evidence.
- The first sampler (GetPixel) was itself a check that could not fail — it blocks for a DWM sync and returns the end state. Caught by the inversion control and replaced; recorded in the doc as another instance of the project's recurring lesson.

## LIMITS — what I could NOT verify

1. **Not confirmed against real Roblox closes.** The harness matches the symptom's shape, magnitude, intermittency and double-rAF immunity, but the live 1-in-3 becoming 0-in-N needs the user counting closes (same protocol as 2026-08-30). I could not drive real closes without injecting input into the live session.

<result>Final report on the stuck-state job:

## What the state actually was — established by measurement

I drove the **real `hud.html`** through a WebView2 harness feeding it the app-choreography messages in five orderings. Two of them reproduce the user's fingerprint exactly (no close animation, no `APPIDLE`, corridor rect stuck in the last `RECTS`): a **stale `APPSHOWN` delivered after `APPCLOSE`**, or after `APPGO`. Mechanism: stale `APPSHOWN` drops the stage mid-close → the stage is `display:none` → the `APPGO` travel runs **no CSS transition** → no `transitionend` → `appAnim` wedges TRUE forever. That single stranded page flag explains all three symptoms: badge dead on both buttons (page gates on `appAnim`; its `APP_EXIT` fallback is ignored by a host whose app mode closed properly), the dead rectangle (`APPIDLE` never sent, so the corridor soft rect never leaves the region while the overlay is no longer click-through), and permanence (every host belt resets host state; nothing resets the page's).

The coordinator's re-entrancy suspicion was tested, not assumed: an LL-hook + injected-click probe showed **0/75 nesting** inside `SetWindowPos`/`force_foreground`/`DwmFlush` (same-process cross-thread owner; cross-process unproven — in limits).

## What changed

- **`web/hud.html`** (load-bearing): stale `APPSHOWN` (`!appOpen`) ignored; early `APPSHOWN` (`appAnim`) deferred via `shownPending` to the travel's end (covers the open-watchdog shape too); `startAppTravelHome` re-stands a downed stage before animating so `APPGO` always yields a real `transitionend`.
- **`src/ui/overlay.cpp`**: `app_open_begin` now has the leg guard its own `WM_HOTKEY` comment claimed; `app_open_finish` clears `g_app_opening` **last**, after `APPSHOWN` is pushed, so no gesture accepted inside it can ever emit `APPCLOSE` ahead of `APPSHOWN`.
- The close-flicker fix is untouched and is now live-confirmed.

## Verification

Pre-fix: 2/5 orderings wedge (the check can fail). Post-fix, same harness against the rebuilt staged page: **5/5 clean** — travel plays, `APPIDLE` arrives, rects return to badge-only, and the previously-clean orderings are unchanged. Build clean; console relaunched (pid 22436) so the user is testing the fixed binary.

## Limits

1. **The live emitter of the stale ordering is not identified** — the page fix makes every candidate emitter produce a recovering close instead of a permanent wedge, but if the user's spam repro still shows a transient oddity, an `ECLIPSE_ZLOG=1` capture will name the emitter from the line order around `APP shown`/`APP close gesture`/`MSG &lt;APP_BOXUP&gt;`.
2. The end-to-end live repro (badge + spam over Roblox) was not reproduced here — it needs real clicks in the user's session. The page half is reproduced exactly; the user re-running their repro is the confirmation that counts.
3. Cross-process hook nesting remains unprobed; the host hardening costs nothing if it never occurs.

Findings appended to `docs/app-close-flicker.md` (status header updated; dead ends recorded, including why a `transitioncancel` listener must NOT be added — it would break the legitimate close-mid-travel self-heal). Harness files deleted per the rule, with rebuild recipes in the doc.</result>

The rule is one line: **the name in the last slot changed → that skill was used.** Any use rotates exactly one name to the end.

Two guards that matter:

- **Character swaps don't fire.** A swap changes the *set* of names, so it re-primes the baseline silently. Comparing whole lists would have reported a phantom use on every swap.
- **First sight doesn't fire** — a joining player gets a baseline, not a toast.

All four Saitama names are in `ULTS[]` at the top of `main.cpp`, and `SHOW_ALL = true` toasts other skills quietly — flip it to `false` for ults only.

Names go in via `textContent`, not `innerHTML` — player-chosen strings from the game never get parsed as markup.

**Click-through** needed a new capability, since a docked panel's rect is reported to the overlay as **solid** on purpose: the overlay owns input there, which is right for the aimbot UI and wrong for a readout. The overlay already had a soft-rect concept (`~` prefix — joins the region so DWM still composites the pixels, but input and cursor belong to the game), so I exposed it:

```c
fx_window_passthrough(1);   // fx.h:280
```

**The context menu** wasn't the page's to fix. `hud.html` already suppresses `contextmenu` on its own document, but a docked snippet is a *cross-origin iframe* — that listener never sees its events, which is why Chromium's Back/Refresh/Inspect menu came up over the game. Killed it on the overlay's core webview instead (`overlay.cpp:2630`), which is the only place that reaches every frame. That fixes it for any docked panel, not just this one.

Rebuilt and relaunched — restart the snippet and try clicking through it.

To answer your question directly: **`fx_window_passthrough` was the right API, but my first implementation only did half the job.** The soft/solid split existed, and I checked that it fed the cursor and the travel click-through — I didn't check that it fed the *ordinary* click path. It doesn't. Outside an app travel the overlay's clicks are decided purely by its window region, and a rect in the region is a place the window exists, so it takes the click regardless of how the page labelled it. That's exactly the failure mode this project's notes warn about: I verified against our own flag instead of the effect.

The fix is a generalisation rather than new machinery. Pointer-following click-through already existed — over a solid piece the overlay is opaque, everywhere else it's `WS_EX_TRANSPARENT` and the click reaches the game — it was just gated to travels. It now runs whenever any soft rect is present. That widens nothing else: with no soft rect the region *is* the solid set, so the region already gives the same answer the pointer rule would.

On `fx_overlay` — good instinct, and it is the genuinely input-free surface (its window returns `HTTRANSPARENT` unconditionally). But it only draws outlined boxes with a name and distance under them: no filled card, no slide-in, no countdown bar. It'd cost you the toast look entirely. Worth keeping in your pocket if the passthrough still misbehaves, though it'd be a different-looking feature rather than the same one.

**Claude**

CSS `pointer-events: none` is the property that makes an element ignore the mouse so the event goes to whatever's behind it — `ui.css` already sets it on `#stack`.

But I was wrong to offer it as the mixed-panel answer, and this session already disproves it: `#stack` has had `pointer-events: none` since the first version, and the panel still wasn't click-through. It only decides which *element inside the page* receives the event. The overlay window has already claimed the click by then, via its region — the game never sees it either way.

So there is currently no page-side way to make part of a docked panel pass through. It's whole-panel `fx_window_passthrough`, or nothing. A mixed panel would need host support that doesn't exist: the docked page reporting its own sub-rects up through the iframe so the overlay could mark the decorative ones soft and the controls solid. That's a real feature, not a CSS trick.

`pointer-events` is still worth using inside a panel for its actual purpose — stopping a decorative overlay element from blocking a button underneath it. It just can't reach past our own window.

Worth doing, and the plumbing is decided by two findings:

- **No page-side option.** The thumbnails API returns no `access-control-allow-origin`, so a `fetch` from the docked iframe's origin is blocked, and the old zero-plumbing `headshot-thumbnail/image` endpoint is **404 — removed**. - **Rate limit is 120/min**, but it batches — `userIds=` takes a comma-separated list, so one request covers the whole server roster. That belongs in the host, not in snippet code where each author would rediscover it.

`fx_player_info.userid` already exists, so there's no memory work at all.

The shape I'd build: `fx_avatar_url(userid, buf, n)` — **non-blocking**, returns empty on first call and kicks off a background batch, returns the URL once cached. Non-blocking is not optional; your loop polls at 15 ms and must never sit on network I/O. Cache lives for the session. Home is `ui/client/avatar.cpp` next to `placename.cpp`, which already owns `http_get` and the Roblox web API, with a sink into a core export so the CLI keeps the same `fx_*` set (a no-op there, like `fx_overlay`).

Two things worth your call before I start:

**Cost.** It's a new core export + sink + a `ui/client` file, so it touches the seams — several files, not a snippet edit. Small, but structural.

**The privacy bit, said plainly:** it makes your machine send the UserIds of everyone in your server to Roblox, from your IP, on a repeating basis. Nothing identifies the console — it's an ordinary public API the site itself uses — but it is new outbound traffic tied to who you're in a game with, where today the app only fetches a place name and offsets. Your call whether that matters.

**User**

lets do both fx_http_get for general purpose and fx_avatar_url for our current stuff. also we could try optimize, but what method would we use?

---

**Claude**

Both, then. On the optimisation question — the answer is layered, and the first layer does almost all the work:

**1. Batch.** `userIds=` takes a comma-separated list, so a whole server is *one* request, not N. That alone takes a 12-player roster from 12 requests to 1 and puts you nowhere near the 120/min limit.

**2. Cache by UserId, and prefetch off the hot path.** Fetch the roster in the background when it changes, not when a toast fires — otherwise the avatar pops in a beat late, which looks broken. Batching makes prefetching nearly free, so lazy-on-toast is the wrong trade here.

**3. Persist the cache across runs.** Note the URL's `30DAY-` prefix — Roblox intends these to be stable for a month. A small file next to `settings.conf` with a TTL means a restart costs zero requests.

**4. Handle `state: "Pending"`.** An uncached avatar returns Pending rather than a URL, and it must be retried later — not cached as a permanent failure. That's a correctness bug, not an optimisation, and it's the one that would bite intermittently.

The two APIs also want *opposite* blocking behaviour, which is the main design point:

Both APIs are in and verified against your live server. Restart the snippet — toasts should now carry the headshot on the left.

**`fx_http_get`** — blocking, on your run's own thread, returns the reply's *full* length so truncation is detectable rather than silent (verified: 190 returned into a 16-byte buffer).

**`fx_avatar_url`** — never blocks, because it's built for the inside of a poll loop. Measured on your server: **12/12 in one batched request**, cached re-ask at 0.003 ms, and a cold start in a fresh process resolved 12/13 from disk in 0.583 ms with **zero requests**. Bogus id correctly refused rather than returning something plausible.

On your optimisation question, the honest answer is that only the first layer matters: batching turns a roster into one request, which puts you at roughly 1/120th of the limit. The disk cache and the `Pending` retry are for latency and correctness, not for rate.

Two things found along the way that weren't part of the ask:

**A real bug in `fx_players`.** `userid` was memoised *together with* the name, and a Player object has a name before it has a UserId — so anyone first seen at the menu got `0` latched for the entire run, with nothing looking wrong: present, correctly named, permanently id-less. Now memoised separately and retried until it lands (`cache.cpp:284`). Your "I wasn't in game" is exactly the case that produced it.

**`http_get` is no longer duplicated.** The WinHTTP implementation moved into `core/features/net.cpp`; `placename.cpp` is now a thin wrapper over it, so the offsets fetch and the new exports share one implementation. I also added a 10 s cap — the default was minutes, and a snippet blocked in `fx_http_get` behind a dead connection would be indistinguishable from a hang. The CLI now links `winhttp` so both binaries still export the same `fx_*` set.

Worth flagging since you'll notice it: the first toast for a player who joins mid-session may briefly have no picture, then have one — the fetch is a second behind the join. Prefetching on roster change keeps that to the join, not to the toast.

Every other member of the `World` struct came back **zero**. A dumper that had actually resolved the World object would have found at least one of them — `Primitives` especially, since it's how the physics world reaches its parts. All-zero-but-one reads as "never resolved the object at all", which is exactly what you'd expect if `Workspace.World` is pointing at the wrong thing. Worth adding as a line: it means the report isn't one bad number, it's the whole struct, and it doesn't require Theo to trust your dumps to see it.

**And yes** — `setfpscap` is UNC, and the funny part is we already have it:

```c
fx_setfps(240);      // fx.h:993
double n = fx_getfps();
```

No injection, no VM, just a write to `TaskScheduler.MaxFPS` behind the arm gate. So the console implements a UNC function without being an executor, which is a decent illustration of how much of that list is really just memory access wearing a Luau costume.

The field name is a lie, incidentally, and it's recorded in `fx.h`: `MaxFPS` is a **double holding the frame period in seconds**, not a frame rate. A client capped at 144 reads `0.006944444`. Read it as a float and you get 0.0 — which looks exactly like an uncapped client.
